Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Begin with the mathematical object: an integer partition. The vector [4,2,1] represents seven as an unordered sum of positive integers. Coins provide a secondary visualization of these part sizes; they are not the subject and there is no optimization objective. We will define partitions, distinguish counting from generation, and develop constrained generators.

Standard form sorts part sizes in nonincreasing order. This is a representation convention, not a restriction on partitions. Weak inequalities preserve repetitions. The number of integer partitions grows rapidly

P(m) counts the partitions of the integer m.

P(m)∼eπ2m34m3

Faster than any polynomial; slower than cᵐ for every fixed c > 1.

The symbol ∼ means the ratio tends to 1 as m grows—not exact equality.

P(1),P(2),P(3),P(4),P(5),P(6)=1,2,3,5,7,11

No simple elementary closed-form formula for P(m) is known. However, its asymptotic growth is known and is shown above. Exact computation is still possible.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
The Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotic formula is P(m) ~ exp(pi sqrt(2m/3))/(4m sqrt(3)): the ratio tends to one as m grows. It implies the book’s coarser Theta(exp(pi sqrt(2m/3))/m) estimate. Neither is an exact equality for a fixed m. Exact algorithms and recurrences exist. Counting gives P(4)=5; enumeration lists its five partitions. No simple elementary closed form is known, which does not mean exact computation is impossible.

3.1 · Generate all partitions: goal and idea

Goal: given a positive integer m, generate every partition of m exactly once, in standard form.

How will we generate them?

1. Try each allowed value for the next part.

2. Recursively partition the remaining sum.

3. Limit later parts to the value just chosen, preserving standard form.

When the remainder is zero, output the completed partition.

State used to implement this idea

Rec(r,B,N)

Introduce Algorithm 3.1 by its purpose, not by a function signature. The input is a positive integer m; outputs are all its partitions, once each, in standard form. N is the current selected-part count; later n denotes a requested constraint. The next slide implements this idea as full pseudocode.

3.1 · Enumerate partitions by recursively selecting parts

Meaning of Rec(r, B, N): generate every completion of the current prefix a[1..N].

Try every positive next part allowed by both the bound and the remainder:

1≤i≤min(B,r)

Store a[N+1] = i; subtract i from the remainder, set the next bound to i, and add one to the part count.

Rec(r−i,i,N+1)

Base case: if r = 0, output only a[1..N] and return.

Rec(m,m,0)

Start: empty prefix, full sum remaining. Invariant: selected-part sum + r = m.

procedure Rec(r, B, N):
    if r == 0:
        output a[1..N]
        return
    for i = 1 to min(B, r):
        a[N + 1] = i
        Rec(r - i, i, N + 1)

3.1 · From the recursion tree to the time bound

Example: every call from Rec(4,4,0). Nodes show the chosen prefix and remainder; green leaves are outputs.

Count leaves and path lengths

V counts calls (nodes): here V=12, with P(4)=5 leaves.

The teal path makes 4 choices. Generally, depth is at most m because every chosen part is positive.

Every node lies on a root-to-leaf path. Summing all path lengths gives an upper bound on the number of nodes.

V≤1+mP(m)
T(m)=O(mP(m))

Search takes O(V); output writing adds at most mP(m) parts. These are upper bounds, not exact operation counts.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
The exact Algorithm 3.1 tree for four has 12 nodes, 11 edges and five leaves. Leaf depths are 4,3,2,2,1, summing to 12. Every non-root node belongs to at least one leaf path, so V≤1+sum(depths)≤1+mP(m). Each edge is one loop choice and recursive call, giving O(V) search overhead. Writing outputs costs the sum of leaf depths as well. Total time is O(mP(m)), an upper bound rather than an exact count or a constant-delay claim.

Correct enumeration: valid, complete and duplicate-free

Validity

Selected-part sum + remainder = m.

Output only at remainder zero.

Completeness

Try every legal next part.

Follow any standard-form partition through its choices.

Uniqueness

Parts remain nonincreasing.

One standard vector has one search path.

Each selected part reduces the remainder by at least one, so every branch terminates.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Validity follows from the sum invariant, positive parts, and nonincreasing order. Completeness: any target partition in standard form has its next part within the current remainder and bound, so the loop can follow its entire vector. Uniqueness: that vector specifies one path; physical coin identity makes no extra choice. Termination follows because every call strictly decreases nonnegative r. This includes [m].

Integer partitions · Definitions & generation

Why does column 1 count the parts?

Every part is positive and every row starts at the left: one first-column dot per row.

Input: 3 parts, so 3 rows

a=[4,2,1]

One coin is one part; three coins make three rows.

Conjugate: largest part is 3

b=[3,2,1,1]

The three first-column dots become the first conjugate row.

Theorem 3.1: partitions of m with exactly n parts and partitions of m with largest part n are equinumerous.
Reason: conjugation is a reversible bijection. Exchanging rows and columns twice restores the original partition.
Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Explain the reason before the notation. The input has three positive parts, 4,2,1. Each part becomes one row, including the part 1. Every left-justified positive row has a dot in column 1. Three rows therefore contribute exactly three first-column dots. Height means the number of dots in that column. Conjugation turns the column into the first output row of length three. No later column can be taller, so the largest output part is three. For any exactly n positive parts or coins, there are n rows and n first-column dots. Conversely, the largest input part four means four columns and hence four output rows or parts. Teal marks input part count to conjugate maximum; blue marks input maximum to conjugate part count. Coin language is an interpretation: each row is a coin, each dot one unit of its value. Both partitions sum to seven. The correspondence holds for every positive partition and is reversible.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Input a is a positive partition in nonincreasing order and b is its conjugate. Subscripts in a_i and b_j are indices, not multiplication. i indexes input rows and j indexes columns. The condition a_i>=j says that input row i has at least j dots, so it reaches column j. The set contains the INDICES of those rows. Vertical bars count set elements, rather than taking the absolute value of a number. At j=2, rows 1 and 2 reach the column; row 3 has length one and does not. The set of row indices is {1,2}, so b_2=2. Its elements are row indices, not the coin values 4 and 2. N counts current input parts and equals three; n in later algorithms denotes a requested constraint and need not equal N. All positive rows reach column one, so b_1=N. The largest input part a_1 is the number of columns and therefore the output length. Conjugating twice returns the input. Under the money interpretation, a_i and b_j are input and new coin values; the mathematics is identical.

3.2 · Conjugate a partition using column heights

Goal: conjugate one partition; new parts are column heights.Input: [4,2,1]. Why conjugate? Convert a maximum-part constraint into a part-count constraint.
a=[4,2,1]
ConjPartition(a[1..N]):
for j = 1 to a[1]:
b[j] = 1
nPrime = a[1]
for i = 2 to N:
for j = 1 to a[i]:
b[j] = b[j] + 1
return b[1..nPrime]

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Algorithm 3.2 transforms ONE partition, not a family. Input a[1..N] is positive and nonincreasing. Its parts are row lengths; output b contains column heights, the conjugate parts. Initialize a[1] columns to one and set nPrime=a[1], the output part count. Each later row i increments columns 1 through a[i]. Return b[1..nPrime]. For [4,2,1], states are [1,1,1,1], [2,2,1,1], then [3,2,1,1]. Initialization, nPrime, both loops, increment, and return are all needed. Each of m cells is counted once: Θ(m) time and Θ(a[1]) output-array space. Distinguish row index i from column index j; coins secondarily display the part sizes.

Count by the number of parts

P(m,n) counts partitions of m into exactly n parts (n coins in the analogy).

P(m)=∑n=1mP(m,n)

Every partition has one definite number of parts. These disjoint groups cover all partitions.

P(6)=1+3+3+2+1+1=11

The six terms correspond to counts 1 through 6.

Boundary values for positive m

P(m,1)=P(m,m)=1
P(m,0)=0,P(0,0)=1
Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
P(m,n) fixes exactly the number of parts, not the largest value. Each partition belongs to exactly one group indexed by n, so summing the group sizes from one to m counts every partition once. At m=6 the group sizes are 1,3,3,2,1,1, giving eleven. For positive m there are no answers when n>m or n<1. The standard boundary convention is P(0,0)=1 and P(m,0)=0 for positive m. In the money version, n is the number of coins, while each part is a coin value. Counting gives a number and does not list the underlying answers.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
For positive m, the exact two-part count is floor(m/2), because the smaller part ranges from one to floor(m/2). The exact three-part count is floor((m^2+4)/12). At m=6 both counts equal three, and each displayed list exhausts that group. For each fixed n, as m tends to infinity, P(m,n)=Theta(m^(n−1)); hidden constants may depend on n. The source image saying fixed m at the end contains a typo: n must be fixed. Thus n=2 is linear and n=3 quadratic. This does not contradict rapid growth of P(m): the number of groups in its sum also grows with m. Do not interpret no general formula as no exact computation; exact recurrences exist. The two formulas and fixed-n order statement are in the supplied source. Conjugation equates the exact-n-part count with the largest-part-n count, motivating the following constrained generator.

Exact counting: one example, two groups

Example: count partitions of 6 into exactly 3 parts. Every partition belongs to exactly one group below.

P(m,n)=P(m−1,n−1)+P(m−n,n)

Group A: at least one part is 1

Remove just one part equal to 1: both the sum and the part count decrease by one.

[4,1,1]→[4,1]
[3,2,1]→[3,2]
P(5,2)=2

Group B: every part is at least 2

Subtract 1 from each of the three parts: the sum decreases by 3; the part count stays 3.

[2,2,2]→[1,1,1]
P(3,3)=1
P(6,3)=P(5,2)+P(3,3)=2+1=3

There is one empty partition: the empty list, with no parts and sum zero. The 1 counts arrangements, not parts.

P(0,0)=1

Removing 1 from [1] leaves the empty list: one valid completion. Impossible cases have count zero.

P(1,1)=P(0,0)+P(0,1)=1+0=1
Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Supplementary counting explanation, not another generation algorithm. Keep m=6,n=3 throughout. The complete family is [4,1,1], [3,2,1], [2,2,2]. Removing just one 1 from the first two gives [4,1] and [3,2]; subtracting 1 from every part of the third gives [1,1,1]. The inverse operations are appending one 1 and adding 1 to every part. Thus the cases are disjoint, exhaustive and reversible, and their counts add to 2+1=3. The general recurrence applies for positive m,n. Negative arguments and n>m have count zero. P(m,0)=0 for positive m; P(0,n)=0 for positive n; P(0,0)=1. Counting returns a number, whereas Algorithms 3.1–3.4 generate the partitions themselves.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Only the initialization wrappers differ; the Rec procedure below them is identical. Algorithm 3.1 begins with no selected parts, the entire target sum remaining, and m as the next-part bound. Algorithm 3.3 first stores n in a[1], so the required largest part is definitely present. It subtracts n from the remaining total, sets the next-part bound to n, and starts with one selected part. Its precondition is 1<=n<=m. For m=7 and n=3, compare state (7,7,0) with (4,3,1), with a[1]=3 already chosen. In Rec, r is the remaining sum, B bounds the next part, and N is the length of the chosen prefix of array a. When r=0, output only a[1..N]; entries beyond N are irrelevant. Otherwise try i from one through min(B,r), write i into position N+1, and recurse with remaining sum r-i and bound i. This bound maintains nonincreasing order, preventing permutations of the same partition. Calling Rec(m,n,0) alone imposes an at-most-n bound but does not require n to occur. For example, with seven and three it also produces [2,2,2,1]. Preselecting n makes the maximum exactly n. When n=m, Rec(0,m,1) immediately outputs [m]. The labels, preconditions and example-state strips are explanatory, not executable lines of the pseudocode. In the money interpretation, a part is a coin value; every positive integer denomination is allowed with unlimited supply. n fixes the largest coin value, not the coin count. The mathematical state and algorithm are unchanged.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
Teaching analysis, not measured timings. Bound search nodes by the sum of root-to-leaf path lengths, each at most m. In 3.2, initialization takes a₁ writes and the later loops sum to m−a₁ increments; hence Θ(m) time and Θ(a₁) additional output space, excluding the existing input. In 3.3 conjugation proves that largest-part-n partitions number P(m,n). In 3.4 add Θ(m) conversion per leaf to the search bound; adding these costs does not change the stated order. Streamed prefixes, stack and current output use O(m) space. These upper bounds do not claim optimality or constant delay.

From target to answers: combine the algorithms

Target: generate every partition of 7 into exactly 3 parts.

Step 1 · 3.3 reuses the recursion of 3.1

Preselect part 3; partition the remaining 4 with bound 3.

a1=3,Rec(4,3,1)

Step 2 · Apply 3.2 to each output

Conjugate each intermediate partition whose largest part is 3; the result has exactly 3 parts.

b=ConjPartition(a)

Algorithm 3.4 is this combination: at each leaf of the 3.3 search, output the conjugate instead of a.

[3,1,1,1,1]→[5,1,1]
[3,2,1,1]→[4,2,1]
[3,2,2]→[3,3,1]
[3,3,1]→[3,2,2]

Left: all largest-part-3 partitions. Right: all exactly-3-part partitions. The bijection preserves completeness and uniqueness.

Kreher & Stinson, Combinatorial Algorithms: Generation, Enumeration, and Search, 1999.

Integer partitionsAmirhossein Mahmoudi
A concrete execution chain, not four disconnected recipes. Convert the requested part-count constraint to a largest-part constraint via conjugation. Algorithm 3.3 changes the initialization of 3.1 rather than generating and filtering all partitions. It produces the four shown intermediate partitions. Algorithm 3.2 conjugates each. Algorithm 3.4 performs that conversion at the recursive leaf, so intermediate answers need not all be stored. Each final answer sums to seven and has exactly three parts. Generally preselect n, call Rec(m−n,n,1), and output its conjugate at each leaf.
